messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: parallel random number generation
parts:
Do we need to worry about this? Malecki had brought
it up before.

I did some reading and the issues are:

1. Thread safety. This isn't an issue for us at
the moment and we could either (a) synchronize, or
(b) use different RNGs in different threads.

2. Independence. The problem is that if you have
an int seed, there are only 4G possibile inits.
If you do a fairly large number of chains (on the
order of 100K), there's a good chance two of them
will be the same.

I don't think either's a problem. But do let me know
if you have more insight than me on this issue.

Given the reparameterization of NUTS, it'll be easy to
plug in Boost's L'Ecuyer RNG.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: parallel random number generation
parts:
I believe the main problem is that if you initialize a plain RNG from
the clock time and you start the chains at essentially the same time,
then the chains are not independent, even if the seeds differ by 1.

A quick and dirty way to mitigate this problem is to take a random
seed independently from /dev/random for each chain. But the rigorous
way is to use the L'Ecuyer RNG.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: parallel random number generation
parts:
I was thinking we'd just take the seed, then use
that to generate a new seed for each chain, then
we'd be good to go.

I don't really see how L'Ecuyer makes that any easier.
Here's a link to the R doc:

http://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/parallel/html/RngStream.html

It could use better examples. The "Details" section
makes it clearer what's supposed to happen -- access up to
7 different substreams, each of which is "independent".
But you need to start by providing 7 seeds. They have
a built-in way to do that, but how's that different than
what I suggested above? How is L'Ecuyer helping?

Boost doesn't give us that kind of functionality for
L'Ecuyer. In particular, I don't see how to get out
multiple streams:

http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_48_0/doc/html/boost/random/ecuyer1988.html

http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_48_0/boost/random/additive_combine.hpp

We still only get operator() for generating variates
as far as I can see.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: parallel random number generation
parts:
There's a simple but computer science oriented PDF of the issues
involved here

http://www.cs.berkeley.edu/~mhoemmen/cs194/Tutorials/prng.pdf

that explains things better than I do.

One approach is to "split" a single stream into say 5 parts for 5
chains. I think most of these approaches to deterministic splitting
rather than splitting at (pseudo) random points because if each chain
needs a lot of pseudo-random numbers and you get unlucky and split at
a bad place, then there could be overlap.

My limited understanding is that the L'Ecuyer algorithm in R is that
is it is better than splitting one stream in the sense that it
actually makes different streams.

Now, if boost doesn't support what R supports, then it's a dead end.
Does this link help you

http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_48_0/libs/mpi/example/parallel_example.cpp

It seems to be a splitting approach rather than (one of) L'Ecuyer.

A more fundamental question is whether you are intending to have stan
take something like a --number_of_chains=5 argument, where the user
would call stan once and stan would spawn 5 threads, one for each
chain. In that case, maybe some form of splitting would work. However,
if you are intending to have stan take something like a --random_seed
argument, where the user would call stan 5 times, then it is up to the
user to supply numbers that do the splitting as appropriately as
possible.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: parallel random number generation
parts:
You can get a little more explanation by executing

vignette("parallel")

in R 2.14.x, especially section 6. I think a big part of L'Ecuyer is
the elegant leaping mechanism. But it also says something I didn't
know, which is that equal width splits are not necessarily optimal.

As far as I can tell, boost just hasn't put a lot of effort into
parallel PRNGs. Are we wedded to boost or just BSD? If the latter,
maybe have a look at http://numbercrunch.de/trng/ .

Ben
